DE-EX-01-001.notes: dass (conjunction, that) starts a clause and sends the verb to the end; das is the article or pronoun. If welches or dieses fits, write das.
DE-EX-01-001.tip: Test: if dieses / welches fits, it's das.

DE-EX-01-002.notes: seid is the ihr form of sein (you are); seit is the preposition 'since'. They sound identical, so only grammar decides.

DE-EX-01-003.notes: tot (dead) is an adjective, written with t; der Tod (death) is a noun, with d and a capital. Compounds follow suit: todmüde, totschlagen.

DE-EX-01-004.notes: ß follows a long vowel or diphthong: Fuß, Straße, heißen. The 1996 reform kept ß in these positions.

DE-EX-01-005.notes: ss follows a short vowel: Fluss, Schloss. Before the 1996 reform it was spelt Fluß. The plural is Flüsse, with ss.

DE-EX-01-006.notes: muss has a short u, so ss. The plural müssen keeps ss, as the vowel stays short. The ich form with ss contrasts with the noun Muße (leisure), long u.

DE-EX-01-007.notes: aß has a long a, so ß; the infinitive essen has a short e, so ss. One verb can switch between the two.

DE-EX-01-008.notes: Languages are nouns and take a capital after verbs and prepositions: Ich spreche Deutsch, auf Deutsch.

DE-EX-01-009.notes: As an adjective before a noun, deutsch is lower-case: die deutsche Sprache. In proper names it's capitalised: die Deutsche Bahn.

DE-EX-01-010.notes: Nominalised adjectives take a capital, even in fixed phrases: im Allgemeinen, im Großen und Ganzen. The rule is often broken in informal writing.

DE-EX-01-011.notes: In Rad fahren, Rad is a noun and is capitalised and written separately. The same goes for Auto fahren.

DE-EX-01-012.notes: A verb used as a noun after bei, zum or beim is capitalised: beim Lesen, zum Kochen. Without the preposition: ich lese, lower-case.

DE-EX-01-013.notes: Two verbs together are normally written separately: spazieren gehen, schwimmen gehen. The noun is one word: das Spazierengehen.

DE-EX-01-014.notes: kennenlernen is written as one word; kennen lernen is also allowed. The participle is kennengelernt.

DE-EX-01-015.notes: Separable verbs are written as one word in the infinitive and participle: zurückgekommen. In the present they split: Er kommt zurück.

DE-EX-01-016.notes: Every subordinate clause is separated by a comma, including dass-clauses. English often has no comma here.

DE-EX-01-017.notes: A zu-infinitive depending on a noun (die Absicht) needs a comma. A comma is also required after um, ohne, statt.

DE-EX-02-001.notes: bekommen means get, receive; werden means become (get + adjective). bekommen is never 'become'. Ich bekomme ein Kind = I'm having a baby.

DE-EX-02-002.notes: ich will means I want (wollen); the future is ich werde. The English 'will' is a false friend. Ich will nach Hause needs no gehen.

DE-EX-02-003.notes: wann asks 'when?' (also in indirect questions); wenn means 'when(ever), if' in conditions and repeated events.

DE-EX-02-004.notes: noch ein means 'one more of the same'; ein anderer means 'a different one'. English 'another' covers both.

DE-EX-02-005.notes: studieren is for university study; lernen is for learning, revising, school. A school pupil lernt, not studiert.

DE-EX-02-006.notes: satt means full after eating. Ich bin voll is colloquial for 'I'm drunk'. The opposite is hungrig, or Hunger haben.

DE-EX-02-007.notes: Du fehlst mir (literally you are missing to me) = I miss you. The person missed is the subject; ich vermisse dich is the direct alternative.

DE-EX-03-001.notes: In southern Germany, Austria and Switzerland, sitzen, stehen and liegen form the Perfekt with sein: Ich bin gesessen. The north uses haben.

DE-EX-03-002.notes: heuer (this year) is standard in Austria and Bavaria. Elsewhere it's dieses Jahr. The adjective is heurig: der Heurige (new wine).

DE-EX-03-003.notes: Swiss Standard German uses -ieren verbs where Germany doesn't: parkieren, grillieren. Germany says parken, grillen.

DE-EX-03-004.notes: Swiss Standard German doesn't use ß: Strasse, gross, Fuss. It's standard there, not an error. Liechtenstein follows the Swiss rule.

DE-EX-03-005.notes: am + nominalised infinitive + sein (the 'Rheinische Verlaufsform') means 'be doing': Ich bin am Arbeiten. It's colloquial nationwide.

DE-EX-03-006.notes: The dative possessive dem Peter sein Auto is widespread in speech but non-standard. Standard: Peters Auto or das Auto von Peter.

DE-EX-03-007.notes: Comparative + wie is common in southern and colloquial speech but non-standard. Standard German uses als.
DE-EX-03-007.text: (Colloquial) Der Film war spannender {{c1::wie::than (colloquial / regional)}} das Buch.
DE-EX-03-007.tr: The film was more exciting than the book.
DE-EX-03-007.flag: dup: replaced Er ist größer wie ich (near-identical to A2-05-009 Er ist größer als ich)

DE-EX-03-008.notes: Spoken Swiss German hardly uses the Präteritum, even for sein: Ich bin gewesen. Germany prefers ich war.

DE-EX-03-009.notes: In Switzerland, anrufen takes the dative (jemandem anrufen). Germany and Austria use the accusative.
DE-EX-03-009.text: (Switzerland) Ich rufe {{c1::dir::du · dative (Swiss: anrufen + dative)}} heute Abend an.
DE-EX-03-009.flag: dup: replaced Ich habe ihm angerufen (near-identical to A1-12-009 Ich habe dich angerufen); answer ihm → dir

DE-EX-03-010.notes: In Switzerland, Radio is masculine: der Radio. In Germany and Austria it's das Radio. Other Swiss gender differences include das Tram.

DE-EX-03-011.notes: Austrian German uses um + price: um zehn Euro (for ten euros). Germany says für. um also means 'around' with times.

DE-EX-03-012.notes: Austrian German says auf Urlaub; Germany says in Urlaub or in den Urlaub. Urlaub machen is used everywhere.

DE-EX-03-013.notes: in der Früh (in the morning) is Austrian and Bavarian. Germany says morgens or am Morgen. Früh here is a noun, so capitalised.

DE-EX-03-014.notes: In Austria, vergessen can take auf + accusative (forget about). Germany uses a direct object. darauf vergessen follows the same pattern.

DE-EX-03-015.notes: Austrian German says am Land (in the countryside); Germany says auf dem Land. The dative am is an + dem.

DE-EX-03-016.notes: In Austria and eastern Germany, viertel vier means 3:15: a quarter of the way to four. Elsewhere it's Viertel nach drei.
DE-EX-03-016.text: (Austria) Der Zug kommt um {{c1::viertel::quarter (Austria / eastern Germany: … vier = 3:15)}} vier.
DE-EX-03-016.tr: The train arrives at quarter past three.
DE-EX-03-016.flag: dup: replaced Es ist viertel vier (near-identical to A1-10-007 Es ist Viertel vor vier)

DE-EX-03-017.notes: In Austria and the south, Cola is often neuter: das Cola. Northern Germany says die Cola. Both genders are in the standard dictionaries.

DE-EX-03-018.notes: Austrian -erl forms diminutives: das Sackerl (bag). Germany uses die Tüte. Other examples: das Busserl (kiss), das Stamperl (shot glass).

DE-EX-03-019.notes: The south says an Ostern, an Weihnachten; the north says zu Ostern. Both are standard. zu and an both take Ostern without an article.

DE-EX-03-020.notes: Swabian uses -le for diminutives: das Häusle. Standard German: das Häuschen. The ending is a famous marker of Swabian speech, as in Spätzle.

DE-EX-03-021.notes: Northern speech splits da-words: Da weiß ich nichts von = Davon weiß ich nichts. It's colloquial. The standard form keeps davon together.

DE-EX-03-022.notes: In speech, weil is often followed by main-clause order (weil ich hab keine Zeit). Writing requires the verb at the end.

DE-EX-03-023.notes: The article before first names (der Peter) is common in southern and colloquial speech. Standard writing omits it.

DE-EX-03-024.notes: brauchen without zu (Du brauchst nicht kommen) is widespread in speech. Standard: Du brauchst nicht zu kommen.

DE-EX-03-025.notes: tun + infinitive (Ich tu grad kochen) is colloquial and regional. Standard: Ich koche gerade. grad is a clipped gerade.
